📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At Microsoft Build 2026, we declared Foundry Managed Compute and Hugging Face models on Foundry — a curated catalog of open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem, refreshed weekly, deployable in one click onto Foundry Managed Compute. Weights are pre-staged in Azure, runtimes are built and scanned by Microsoft, and every model in the Collection ships with the same enterprise security, governance, observability, and billing that applies to every other model on Foundry.

Microsoft Foundry is a platform for building and operating agentic AI applications. Foundry starts with the widest model selection on any cloud — models from Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, Hugging Face, and others, spanning frontier, open-source, and custom weights — all accessible through a single endpoint and a single set of SDKs in Python, C#, JavaScript, and Java.

On top of those models sits the Foundry Agent Service: multi-agent orchestration with built-in memory, knowledge grounding through Foundry IQ, and a catalog of connectable tools via agentic protocols, so agents can work with enterprise data. Once agents are running, Foundry provides end-to-end tracing, real-time monitoring, continuous evaluations, and a prompt optimizer that improves agent behavior based on eval results — observability and quality loops that are part of the platform.

Alongside that, developers get access to:.

Alongside pay-per-token (lowest-friction path to get started) and provisioned throughput (predictable, high-performance production workloads on frontier models), Foundry Managed Compute is the third deployment option in Foundry: a managed GPU platform-as-a-service for open-source and custom models.

You deploy a model instance described by the things that matter to your workload — parameter count, context length, and whether you want to optimize for latency or throughput — and Foundry handles the GPU topology underneath, whether the instance lands on one accelerator or several, so you think and plan in model terms.

Microsoft takes care of the machine: container updates, runtime upgrades, and security patches happen automatically on the supported runtimes — vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, NIM, TEI, llama.cpp — without redeploying your model, while model configuration, deployment behavior, and routing stay with you.

That consistency carries through the developer surface — pay-per-token, provisioned throughput, and Managed Compute share:.

Open-source models integrate with Foundry Agents the same way frontier models do, so you can mix model types in a single agent without a separate integration path.

Industry observers note that same code, same workflow. Quota is aligned to accelerator families, so a plan built on the H100 family today carries forward as new hardware generations come online.

Sources indicate that hugging Face is the public square of open AI: 15 million builders, 400,000 organizations, and over 3 million open models published, with newly introduced frontier capabilities — agentic coding, video segmentation, speech, embeddings — landing weekly. It's the GitHub of open models, where the community publishes weights, writes model cards, compares evaluations, and pulls models for experimentation.

Open models have closed the gap with proprietary models on benchmark after benchmark, and they unlock things proprietary endpoints can't:.

Recent findings suggest that the catch has always been the operational layer: discovery, license review, security screening, runtime selection, GPU sizing, image building, CVE patching, and standing the model up behind an enterprise-grade endpoint. Hugging Face, by itself, is not an enterprise serving platform. Hugging Face models on Foundry is that operational layer, run by Microsoft.

The Hugging Face Collection brings a curated subset of models directly into the Foundry Model Catalog:.

From your side, an open-weight model in the Hugging Face Collection looks and behaves like any other model in the Foundry Model Catalog, and every model in the Collection has been put through a multi-stage publishing pipeline before it ever shows up there.

Hugging Face and Microsoft work together to bring the most popular open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem to Microsoft Foundry — production-ready for enterprise environments — through a systematic curation process:.

Because weights are pre-staged in Azure storage and runtime images live in a Microsoft-managed registry, your deployments won't need outbound network access to Hugging Face Hub — you can deploy to production inside a private network.

Hugging Face models on Foundry are powered by a versatile collection of community-built, open-source inference runtimes — each selected and tuned for Foundry Managed Compute, and matched to the model architectures it serves best. Across all runtimes, the systematic curation process means newly introduced versions and patches land on Foundry swiftly, and existing model deployments are upgraded automatically — without requiring you to redeploy.

Recent findings suggest that vLLM — the default high-throughput serving engine for open large language models, tuned for production GPU workloads. Because Hugging Face is a direct contributor to vLLM, any model in the Transformers library can run on vLLM out of the box — so when a new model lands on Hugging Face, it can be served on Foundry the same day, with no waiting on a custom integration.

SGLang — a serving engine for language and multi-modal models, with strong support for structured outputs (JSON, regex, grammar-constrained generation) that agentic and tool-using workloads depend on. Hugging Face and the SGLang team have built a Transformers backend integration for SGLang, so any model in the Transformers library runs on SGLang out of the box — and reaches Foundry the same day it lands on Hugging Face.

Recent findings suggest that text Embeddings Inference (TEI) — the runtime for embedding, reranker, and sequence-classification models. Accelerator-specific images ship with kernels compiled for each GPU and CPU family Foundry supports, keeping the embedding hot path lean for RAG and semantic-search workloads.

Recent findings suggest that llama.cpp — the CPU and small-GPU path for GGUF-quantized models. Useful for cost-optimized deployments, smaller models, and CPU-only regions, with the same OpenAI-compatible API as vLLM and SGLang.

TensorRT-LLM and NIM — used on NVIDIA hardware where NVIDIA's optimized kernels and Triton-based serving deliver meaningfully better latency or throughput for specific model families.

hf-serve — Hugging Face's own multi-model inference server, used for model architectures outside the LLM and embedding fast paths (vision, audio, segmentation, and other Transformers-native pipelines) so the Collection can cover every modality with a consistent serving layer.

The Hugging Face Collection in the Foundry Model Catalog is where you start, and deployment is five steps:.

A deployment template is the unit of choice in step 2: a named, versioned asset that pins the runtime, the accelerator family and count, the context length, and the runtime-specific tuning needed to serve the model well — so picking a template is the only knob you turn for "how do I want this model to run.".

qwen3-32b, for example, ships with four templates the deploy wizard exposes side by side:.

Each template arrives pre-tuned for the model — runtime settings, tool-call and reasoning parsers, scoring path, health probes, request concurrency, and any model-specific context-extension settings are all set by Microsoft, with any trade-offs called out inline in the template description. When you script the deploy, you reference the template and Foundry handles the rest.

The deployment is reachable through the unified Foundry endpoint with the OpenAI SDK — the `model` field takes the deployment name you just created:.

A chat-completions model from the Collection slots into Foundry Agents as an admin-connected model and is callable through the Foundry Responses API with the same OpenAI SDK — same auth, same endpoint, same observability.

Available now in preview: the Hugging Face Collection in the Microsoft Foundry Model Catalog — thousands of models across every modality, refreshed weekly, deployable onto Foundry Managed Compute with NVIDIA A100, NVIDIA H100, or AMD MI300X accelerators in Global and Data Zone scopes, behind a unified Foundry endpoint with Playground support, first-class Azure Monitor metrics, per-deployment billing tags, and curated runtime upgrades and CVE patching applied automatically to your deployments.

On the roadmap: broader coverage of the Hugging Face ecosystem, additional accelerator families, and Bring Your Own Weights for fine-tuned and proprietary variants deployed through the same templates and governance as Collection models.

Recent findings suggest that hugging Face is where open models are published and discovered. Microsoft Foundry is where enterprises operationalize them — on curated, license-screened, security-screened weights hosted in Azure; on community-built and CVE-scanned runtimes; behind a single endpoint with enterprise identity, networking, observability, and agent integration on top. The breadth of the open-source ecosystem, with the operational layer Microsoft runs underneath. 📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two security events landed side by side this week, PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise.
  • PHP2Shell is a pair of critical flaws in the PHP engine itself, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.
  • According to recent reports, the eMudhra compromise is a different kind of problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two security events landed side by side this week, PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Both reached the same place, the foundation their applications are built on.

PHP2Shell is a pair of critical flaws in the PHP engine itself, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. They let an unauthenticated request become code execution on the server, on any PHP application, however careful its own code is, and PHP runs about 69% of the websites whose server-side language is known.

According to recent reports, the eMudhra compromise is a different kind of problem. Eight intermediate certificates from the certificate authority eMudhra turned out to have private keys that can be computed from the public certificates, which let anyone glitch a certificate for any website and have it accepted. Browsers revoke certificates like these on their own, but a container image carries its own trust store and keeps trusting them until it is rebuilt.

The dhi.io/php image was rebuilt on the patched PHP and published early on October 22, within 24 hours of the upstream release and after the DHI testing and verification steps. Pulling the current tag puts you on the fixed version. The few DHI images that bundle their own PHP application, such as composer and nextcloud, follow as their upstream projects release.

Recent findings suggest that the certificate compromise touched the whole catalog, because every image carries a trust store. In the 48 hours after the PHP release, the DHI build system ran 16,567 package and image builds across the catalog. By 10pm UTC on October 22, almost all catalog tags were on the fixed CA store, with most of the rest in the build queue. That percentage comes from the SBOM that ships with every image, read for every published tag to check which CA store and which PHP version it carries, and you can run the same check on anything you pull.

If you run PHP on Docker Hardened Images, pull the current tag for your branch and redeploy, and rebuild anything you built on top of a DHI image so it picks up the newly introduced base docker pull dhi.io/php:8.4.

In a recent development, customizations built through the DHI Enterprise workflow are rebuilt automatically when the base layer is patched. For the certificate fix the same applies to every image you build from a DHI base, PHP or not. The Docker Security enhancement from October 22 lists the affected PHP versions and the support path.

If you run PHP in any other container, check the PHP version running inside it rather than the tag on the outside, and rebuild it on a patched base.

Weeks like this one will keep coming, but a trusted foundation will make all the difference.

If you are not building on hardened images yet, this week is the wake-up call and the week to start. Both events landed on the foundation, and that is where the fix has to happen, in the image itself, rebuilt from fixed sources before anyone pulls it.

This is exactly what Docker Hardened Images were built for. Docker builds, patches and maintains the system packages inside each image from source, and the build system is event-driven, so an upstream release or a changed package triggers rebuilds of everything that depends on it. Each image ships signed, with its SBOM, SLSA Build Level 3 provenance and VEX data attached, which is why a rebuild of this size can be measured as well as done.

Recent findings suggest that the catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, with near-zero CVEs on every image. It stays compatible with the Alpine and Debian your teams already run, so adoption is a one-line change to the FROM line in your Dockerfile, with no migration project attached. DHI Select and DHI Enterprise add SLA-backed remediation with critical CVE fixes within 7 days, FIPS and STIG variants, image customization with the guarantees kept, and Extended Lifecycle Support for the versions upstream has stopped patching. All of it is in the Docker Hardened Images catalog, free to pull today.

Principal Product Marketing Manager, Docker.

Vishrut Iyengar is Principal PMM for Security at Docker, focused on Docker Hardened Images, supply chain security, and securing what AI agents build.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the partnership expands the choices available in Microsoft Foundry while bringing video into the broader platform developers use to build AI applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that video workloads do not all start with the same input or aim for the same result. A creative team might explore several interpretations of a written brief. A retailer might turn an approved product image into a short motion concept. An application developer might combine image generation and video generation into a workflow that takes an idea from description to frame to scene. Each scenario brings different requirements for visual quality, motion, creative control, turnaround time, and cost. All of this means that a multi-model solution is necessary to realize a full vision.

According to recent reports, today, Microsoft and fal are helping developers find the right tools for their workloads. We are excited to announce that Kling, LTX, and MiniMax video models are rolling out to in public preview in Microsoft Foundry through our new partnership with fal. Available as a first-party Azure service, these text-to-video and image-to-video options give creators and developers more ways to utilize video generation with the experiences they want to build.

Recent findings suggest that the partnership expands the choices available in Microsoft Foundry while bringing video into the broader platform developers use to build AI applications. The goal is to let developers pick the right model for each step of an experience, then connect those steps into a working application.

Sources indicate that “fal has seen incredible adoption this year alone with generative media across all industries from advertising to marketing to gaming. Partnering with Microsoft allows both of us to truly enable the wide creative ecosystem and ensure that all AI solutions that lean on generative media, becomes a multi-model one.” - Burkay Gur, Cofounder.

Recent findings suggest that fal is the full stack for generative media, built for creators and developers, with APIs for over 1500 models across image, video, audio, 3D, and generative worlds. As a truly encapsulating platform, fal provides inference, training, and infrastructure to run generative media workloads in production, while also providing innovative post trained models that pushes the boundaries on speed and quality.

That specialization matters because generative media is both a creative and an engineering workload. A compelling demo is only the start. Production applications also need to handle real traffic, scale with demand, and balance output quality, latency, and cost.

According to recent reports, through this partnership, developers will be able to access a selected set of video models in Microsoft Foundry, served by fal and sourced from the companies that build them. The initial portfolio gives teams a choice of models for different creative requirements instead of relying on one model for every task, with more models planned over time.

According to recent reports, the initial portfolio spans Kling v3 Pro, LTX-2.5 Fast, LTX-2.5 Pro, MiniMax H3 Max, and MiniMax H3 Max Turbo. These models give developers different starting points for generating video from text and animating existing images. A team rapidly exploring creative concepts may prioritize speed and cost, while a team producing fewer, higher-fidelity assets may weigh output quality more heavily. Whether an application starts from text or an existing image, and what it needs in output quality and cost, also shapes the choice.

Kling: From a still image to a directed scene.

Kling v3 Pro combines cinematic visuals and fluid motion with native audio generation and custom element support. Its image-to-video capabilities give developers control over how a starting image becomes a moving scene, a fit for applications that prioritize visual direction and motion.

LTX: One model for fast drafts, one for final output.

In a recent development, for rapid iteration and previews, LTX-2.5 Fast is the speed-optimized option; for high-fidelity final output, LTX-2.5 Pro is the quality-optimized option. Both support text-to-video and image-to-video generation with synchronized audio.

MiniMax: Another approach to video generation.

Sources indicate that miniMax H3 Max and MiniMax H3 Max Turbo are post-trained variants of MiniMax H3 focused on prompt adherence, aesthetics, and inference performance. For developers, they provide additional options to evaluate against an application’s creative brief, quality requirements, and performance needs.

Recent findings suggest that “When building with video models, the details matter: how closely the output follows your prompt, how well it preserves your reference images/videos/audios and how swiftly you can try another idea. Kling gives developers control over detailed reference to video generation. LTX offers fast iteration and high-quality output through its Fast and Pro variants. H3 Max brings fal's post-training and inference optimizations to improve quality and speed. Having these models available through Microsoft Foundry gives developers more flexibility to choose what works best for the application they are building." - Gökay Aydoğan, Creative Engineer.

Sources indicate that bringing video generation into an enterprise application requires more than choosing the right model. Teams need a platform where they can evaluate different options, build with the models that fit their requirements, and operate those experiences alongside the rest of their applications.

According to recent reports, the initial portfolio of video models is hosted in the US, and Microsoft Foundry is the first provider to offer a US-hosted Kling 3 endpoint. Key considerations for enterprise teams:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Version 4.0 of Redmond’s cloudy OS is free to use in its cloud.
  • Microsoft has issued version 4.0 of its very own Azure Linux, which it built atop Fedora for the first time and now suggests is ready to run mainstream workloads.
  • Redmond’s history with Linux is long and tangled.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Version 4.0 of Redmond’s cloudy OS is free to use in its cloud. Repeat. Free to use.

Microsoft has issued version 4.0 of its very own Azure Linux, which it built atop Fedora for the first time and now suggests is ready to run mainstream workloads.

Redmond’s history with Linux is long and tangled. Former CEO Steve Ballmer infamously labelled the project a cancer but by 2015 Microsoft had quietly adapted the OS to power some switches in its Azure Cloud.

Microsoft then built some of its own Azure services on containers and created a lightweight Linux for them to run in. In 2020, Microsoft released that Linux as CBL-Mariner, largely so that developers who used services like Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) that relied on the OS could access the platform they were building for.

In a recent development, in 2022, CBL-Mariner became Azure Linux 2.0, another container-centric lightweight release. Version 3.0 followed in 2024, now billed as ready for “broad Azure usage” with Azure Kubernetes Service.

According to recent reports, in June 2026, Microsoft announced version 4.0 and billed it as suitable for Azure Virtual Machines, VM Scale Sets, and container images. The massive change that made that repositioning possible was basing the OS on Fedora rather than Microsoft’s own Common Base Linux.

Microsoft also tuned the Linux kernel – version 6.18 LTS – by adding Hyper-V guest drivers and other features that make it behave well in Azure. It also natively supports tools like Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Monitor, and the Azure CLI, which Microsoft reckons committed Azure consumers already employ and therefore want to apply to their cloudy Linux workloads.

Or as Redmond puts it: “the familiarity of [the] RPM package ecosystem, while adding Azure-native security, compliance, and operational capabilities.”.

All of those changes add up to an OS that Microsoft says is worth a look “Whether you're running web applications, databases, or GPU-accelerated AI/ML workloads.”.

Redmond makes that recommendation in part because Azure Linux comes with “no additional OS licensing cost.” Other commercial Linux distributions will cost users money, meaning Microsoft can now make an argument that SUSE and RHEL subscriptions might be superfluous for both AKS users and those who use Azure to host other applications on Linux.

In a recent development, azure Linux 4.0 debuted last Thursday and is available here. Redmond’s latest Linux debuted just days after Microsoft issued a monster upgrade to version 3.0. ®.

It has been revealed that with the launch of a one-click Studio landing experience, choosing Customize on SageMaker AI or Deploy on SageMaker AI on a supported Hugging Face model page takes you directly to the console. SageMaker AI then automatically provisions a upcoming domain with pre-configured permissions in seconds and carries the model context through.

This launch introduces three capabilities that shorten the path from a Hugging Face model to a working SageMaker Studio workflow.

When you browse models on Hugging Face, you’ll now see action buttons alongside supported models that map directly to SageMaker Studio workflows:.

Each entry point preserves the context, meaning you don’t need to search for the model again once inside Studio.

Recent findings suggest that latest Studio environments created through this flow come with permissions already configured for the full range of SageMaker AI capabilities, including model customization, training jobs, notebook experimentation, and endpoint deployment. A new managed policy, AmazonSageMakerModelCustomizationCoreAccess, is created and attached for you. It provides permissions for serverless model customization jobs using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), with supported deployment to SageMaker AI or Amazon Bedrock endpoints. On the Hugging Face model page, click on “Deploy” and select “Amazon SageMaker AI”. If the model is supported, you will see two buttons, “Deploy on SageMaker AI” and “Customize on SageMaker AI”. Then select “Customize on SageMaker AI” for a supported model.

After you deploy your endpoint, test inference directly from Studio’s endpoint testing interface.

In a recent development, user interactions with agents today are where computers were in the terminal era: capable, and answering almost everything in text. Customers can ask an agent for anything by typing or talking, and what comes back is usually a wall of text, a poor way to compare three products or edit and approve a detailed plan.

It has been revealed that today, we're releasing A2UI 1.0, the first stable version of our open protocol for generative UI. It lets AI agents answer with interactive screens, such as a form to confirm or a chart. Developers can use it now with open-source renderer SDKs for the web, Android, and iOS and agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. Companies such as Atlassian, Alation, Bloomberg, and ByteDance are already building with it.

Recent findings suggest that with A2UI, the agent describes what to show, and every app draws the UI with its own native components. The application receives A2UI messages and each app renders the content securely and at native speed. People get the same low latency, high trust, and complete native fidelity whether they reach a tech giant's agent in its own app or in a third-party AI assistant that hosts MCP apps, such as Gemini or Claude.

You wake up sick. Getting through the morning takes six apps: book a video visit, move your meetings, tell your team, turn on an out-of-office reply, ask your partner to do school pickup and order soup. Ask a text-only agent instead, and you get a numbered wall of text, then round after round of “which ones?”. A2UI won't handle your sick day, but it gives developers the framework to build an agent that can. That agent could answer with one view of all six apps. Changing your proposal is a couple of taps instead of another round of messages, and nothing is sent until you confirm.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nobody died, money got made, and the maintenance crew didn’t care.
  • If you've made mistakes at work that threatened to torch your career, The Register has just the column for you.
  • Today, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Axl" who once worked at a petrol station (aka a gas station for US readers).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nobody died, money got made, and the maintenance crew didn’t care.

If you've made mistakes at work that threatened to torch your career, The Register has just the column for you. We call it Who, Me?, we print one every Monday, and you're reading this week's instalment!

Today, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Axl" who once worked at a petrol station (aka a gas station for US readers).

One Friday afternoon, in the shadow of a holiday weekend, the PC that drove the station's pumps and point of sale stopped working, leaving it unable to operate.

Axl called the manufacturer and got the very unwelcome news that a technician could visit on Tuesday at the earliest.

As the petrol station was in a spot that would attract a few weekend tourists, the potential losses were substantial, and Axl felt he needed to act.

Industry observers note that he knew the main computer lived inside a large metal box affixed to a wall, an arrangement that meant electronics and flammable vapors were always kept well apart. The machine's power switch was accessible, so Axl turned it off and on again – and watched the machine come back to life, before shutting itself down five minutes later.

That behavior was a strong hint that something was overheating but confirming that theory was not easy because the metal case included a lock (see previous remarks about preventing fires) and Axl didn't have they key.

Axl inspected the hinges on the box, found they were held on with screws and was able to remove the lid and access the PC.

"Aside from the considerable amount of dust and hair inside, I could see that the CPU fan was not turning," he wrote. "Either it had failed or was not receiving the control signal to cool.".

The service station had an office out the back. Axl liberated a desk fan, pointed it at the PC, and watched it come alive again.

An hour later, the PC was still working, so Axl decided he needed a fix that would last the weekend.

"I drove to a local electrical shop and purchased a high speed bathroom extraction fan which I rigged up inside the case, then closed it up best I could with tape and cardboard," he told The Register.

That rickety rig kept fuel flowing for three days.

Industry observers note that "On Tuesday afternoon, the support engineer arrived and I explained how I kept us in business over the weekend," Axl wrote. "He just shrugged his shoulders, smiled and changed the failed fan. I didn't even get the 'It's our kit, leave it alone' lecture.".

He did get the satisfaction of a job well done.

"No one died from an exploding petrol station and the tourists were happy they could go home," he wrote.

Industry observers note that have you made a risky fix in a dangerous place? If so, the safe option is to click here and send your story to Who, Me? We promise to handle it with care and hopefully share it on some future Monday. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, TL;DR: The transformers vLLM backend is now as fast (or faster) than custom vLLM implementations for many LLM architectures.
  • Recent findings suggest that the transformers library has become the reference modeling library for Machine Learning.
  • Sources indicate that we have fully embraced this role in the ecosystem and are investing a lot of effort to make it easier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, TL;DR: The transformers vLLM backend is now as fast (or faster) than custom vLLM implementations for many LLM architectures. Model authors can automatically leverage their transformers implementations to get ultra fast vLLM inference, for free.

Recent findings suggest that the transformers library has become the reference modeling library for Machine Learning. It supports 450+ architectures through consistent APIs, and is designed with the main goal that model implementations are self contained and easy to understand. Going through transformers code makes it easy for contributors to learn how an architecture works, and then port it to other frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, MLX, llama.cpp, and many others.

Sources indicate that we have fully embraced this role in the ecosystem and are investing a lot of effort to make it easier. A big step in this direction was the integration last year of transformers as a modeling backend in vLLM. This has been allowing model authors to run transformers models (LLMs and VLMs alike) inside vLLM, without having to port anything. Transformers provides the modeling code, and vLLM provides extremely optimized inference techniques such as continuous batching and custom attention kernels.

This integration gets better now 🚀!

We put the transformers modeling backend for vLLM head to head with vLLM's hand written native implementations across three very different Qwen3 models:.

Industry observers note that running any* Hugging Face model through the transformers modeling backend is a single flag — --model-impl transformers. It composes with the usual parallelism options, so nothing about your serving setup changes:.

In a recent development, *Models that use linear attention are not currently supported, but they will be soon! Custom models where the code lives in a Hub repo are unlikely to work as they will not have been written compliantly.

Each model is compared under three conditions that are identical in every way except the code path:.

The full, reproducible runner is available as a gist: benchmark.sh.

The transformers modeling backend for vLLM used to focus on attention as the bottleneck for inference. By plugging vLLM’s attention implementation at runtime, we could make a transformers model run efficiently inside the vLLM engine. But there are many dimensions to deployments that only a custom port can target to extract maximum inference performance. Parallelization across GPUs, compilation, fused kernels, and many more, all contribute to leveraging your hardware to achieve ultra-fast inference.

When model authors wanted the absolute best performance, they were still writing custom vLLM implementations.

The latest iteration of the transformers modeling backend for vLLM dynamically applies inference specific layer fusions at runtime to match the speed of custom code implementations, for compatible architectures.

In a recent development, the transformers modeling backend for vLLM now uses torch.fx to perform static analysis on the model’s graph. This process searches for known patterns that can be optimised. After any patterns have been identified, it uses ast (abstract syntax tree) to manipulate the source code and rewrite some of the operations in place.

As shown above, this results in native vLLM inference speed for compatible models, without having to write a single line of code to optimize the model for inference.

We are in the process of writing a detailed blog post to dive deep inside these optimized inference methods and explain in detail how we manipulate the model to adapt to them.

One provenance implication here is that the model definition and the executed inference graph are no longer the same artifact boundary.

If the runtime rewrites model code and replaces modules with fused kernels, deployment evidence probably needs to preserve both the source model identity and the transformation/runtime path.

  • It has been revealed that this story is the opposite.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is Part 6 of our AI Coding Agent Horror Stories series, where we look at real security incidents involving AI coding agents and at how Docker Sandboxes contain agent execution at the boundary rather than at the command line.

In a recent development, every story in this series so far has been about an agent reaching for something it should not have touched. We have seen agents wander into home directories, drop production databases, leak credentials, and run shell commands that did something very different from what the developer expected. In each case, the damage came from the agent having more reach than it needed.

It has been revealed that this story is the opposite. The agent in this one reached nothing at all, because it was deliberately built so that it could not. And yet, on the night in question, it was still the most dangerous thing in the pipeline.

This story was shared by Pratik Kumar Singh as part of our Agent Hall of Shame contest on social media.

A platform engineer built a code review bot for his team. The idea was simple and useful. Every time someone pushes code, the bot reads what changed and writes a review into the pipeline, the same kind of first pass a human teammate would give before a person looks at the change.

Industry observers note that he named the bot BuaJi. In India, your bua is your father’s sister, and in many families she is the relative who inspects everything you do and always manages to find something wrong with it. For a code reviewer, it is a fitting name.

Industry observers note that what made BuaJi interesting was how carefully it was set up. The bot runs on local models through Ollama, which means the model weights sit on the engineer’s own hardware and no request ever goes out to an AI vendor. It also runs as a job in his CI pipeline, triggered whenever someone pushes code. Taken together, this makes the whole setup self-hosted. The code it reads is manufacturer source code, and with this design none of it ever leaves the building. That was a deliberate choice, because his company takes that seriously.

He also gave BuaJi one firm rule: it can read, and it can comment, and that is all. It cannot run terraform apply, which is the command that creates or changes real cloud infrastructure. It cannot run kubectl apply, which changes what is actually running in the Kubernetes cluster. And it cannot push a commit, so it has no way to change the code itself. Those are the commands that change the real world, and BuaJi was given none of them. On paper, this is exactly how you would want an AI reviewer to be built.

It has been revealed that the version of BuaJi in the companion repo is a deliberately minimal reviewer. It checks Go files against a handful of style rules. The report below is the kind of free-form finding any reviewer produces once you let it comment in prose rather than pass/fail, which is exactly the direction these bots get pushed in practice.

Recent findings suggest that his product ships with a bundled copy of PostgreSQL. Older PostgreSQL releases have published vulnerabilities with CVE numbers attached, and upgrading to a newer patch release is how you make those known concerns go away. So he bumped the version.

Sources indicate that this is about as boring and as responsible as a code change gets. It touches a few lines, it changes a version number, and its only purpose is to close security holes that are already public. Any reviewer, human or machine, should look at it and approve it in a few seconds. There is nothing in that diff to be suspicious about, and that is precisely why what happened next matters.

According to recent reports, buaJi responded with roughly fifteen hundred words rejecting the change. For context, a normal review comment is a sentence or two.

Recent findings suggest that the report described the version bump as an “architectural takeover,” a structural change smuggled into the codebase under the cover of routine maintenance. It claimed that the newly introduced PostgreSQL build was a vehicle for sending internal data to a third-party organization, and it named that company outright. The company does not exist.

In a recent development, it went further. It referred to specific Kubernetes resources by name, as though it had inspected the cluster and found them. Those resources had never existed, and BuaJi had no access to the cluster that would have let it look. It then wrote Go scripts to “isolate the infected PostgreSQL nodes,” even though nothing was infected. Finally, it told the engineer to revoke all IAM access immediately, an action that would lock out every person in the organization, including the people who would be needed to fix any real problem.

Recent findings suggest that holding the whole argument together was a CVE number that has never been issued by anyone. Of everything in the report, this is the detail worth pausing on. A CVE identifier is one of the easiest things in security to verify, since you can look it up in a public registry in a few seconds. The bot invented a fact in the one place where invented facts are easiest to catch.

Recent findings suggest that and yet the report looked completely convincing. The Markdown was clean and well structured. The YAML it proposed would have parsed without errors. The tone was urgent and confident, the way a senior security engineer writes when they have found something serious and need you to act before it gets worse. The engineer spent about two minutes reading the CI logs, realized that none of it was real, and went back to what he was doing.

Caption: Comic illustrating how a confident, well-formatted security report from an AI reviewer can be entirely fabricated, and what happens when somebody acts on it.

In a recent development, it is important to say clearly that the read-only rule did its job. BuaJi could not carry out any of its own recommendations, and it never had any access to the cluster. Because of that, the entire episode cost the engineer two minutes of his evening and nothing more.

Recent findings suggest that the trouble is that the rule only controlled what BuaJi could do. Nobody had thought about what BuaJi could say. A read-only agent is still allowed to tell people what to do, and the person reading its output usually has exactly the access that the agent was denied. BuaJi could not run the scripts it wrote, but it could write them down and hand them to someone who could.

Recent findings suggest that this engineer caught the problem because he knows his own cluster well. He knew those Kubernetes resources were not real and that nothing had been compromised. Now imagine a newer engineer on call at two in the morning, half awake, looking at a long and alarming security report in the pipeline. Revoking all IAM access in production in the middle of the night is an outage all by itself. Running an unreviewed Go script against your database nodes could be considerably worse. In both scenarios, BuaJi would not have done anything. A person would have done all of it, in good faith, because the report told them to.

According to recent reports, what makes this so hard to defend against is that no permission model would have flagged it, because no permission was ever violated. The agent stayed within its boundary. The engineer had every right to run those commands on his own systems. The only thing in the entire chain that was false was the content of the report.

Here’s the honest part: a sandbox is not a fact-checker. No microVM boundary will ever make a review comment accurate. What a boundary changes is what that fabricated output can do once it exists.

It has been revealed that remember where BuaJi’s read-only rule actually lived, in a convention. One engineer configured it in his own pipeline and has to keep remembering to leave it in place. Rules like that hold until someone is in a hurry, or a new teammate copies the config and drops a section they did not understand, or a small exception made for a good reason quietly becomes permanent. None of this needs bad intent; it is just how real teams work.

Docker Sandboxes run agents inside isolated microVMs each with its own kernel, its own filesystem, and a network that denies everything by default. An agent inside one can invent anything it likes, but the invention has nowhere to go: no credentials to use, no cluster to reach, no commit to push, unless someone allowed that access ahead of time. The read-only rule stops being something a person remembers and becomes a property of the environment. And when a report claims it inspected your cluster, the policy log is your proof it never could have.

It has been revealed that that protects you from the agent. It does nothing for the human who reads the output, and no sandbox ever will. For that half, treat agent review output the way you already treat agent input, untrusted until something checks it: label it so it doesn’t carry a colleague’s weight, verify any CVE numbers, and never run agent-written remediation until a person has read and understood it.

This is the same pattern as the sandbox escapes Pillar published in July. The boundary itself was never broken; a file was written inside the sandbox, and a tool outside later trusted it. An agent’s output is always an input to whatever reads it next and somewhere downstream, something trusts what it receives. Very often, that something is a person.

It has been revealed that let’s move BuaJi into a Docker Sandbox, one step at a time. By the end, the read-only rule is enforced by the environment, not by memory.

According to recent reports, buaJi is a small Python script, buaji.py. Its GitLab job installs Ollama on a GPU runner, starts ollama serve, loads the model named in LLM, and runs the script.

Recent findings suggest that the script reads review rules from rules.md and finds the changed files with git diff HEAD^ HEAD --name-only. It sends each file and rule to Ollama at http://localhost:11434 and prints the answers to the CI log.

Sources indicate that the catch is that everything shares one container: the model, the script, the checkout and every CI variable, including CI_JOB_TOKEN. BuaJi is read-only only because the script happens not to write anything.

We split the job in two. The model stays on the runner next to the GPU. BuaJi moves into a microVM that can read the code, talk to the model, and nothing else.

One open path to the model, everything else blocked, and a CVE check on the way out.

It has been revealed that inside a sandbox, localhost is the sandbox itself. So we read the Ollama address from an environment variable and keep the old value as the default:.

Outside a sandbox, nothing changes. Inside one, we point OLLAMA_URL at the runner.

Today the job runs apt-get and pip3 install on every run, which needs internet access each time.

Instead, build a small image once with everything BuaJi needs, so the sandbox never downloads anything:.

Push it to your registry and store its name in a CI variable called BUAJI_TEMPLATE.

Ollama stays on the runner with the GPU. Install it once on the runner instead of running curl | sh in every pipeline.

The model never enters the sandbox. BuaJi reaches it through one port, opened in Step 5.

This step decides what BuaJi can see and change.

Notice what is missing: no GitLab token, no kubeconfig, no cloud credentials. Even if BuaJi tried kubectl or terraform, it would have nothing to connect with.

Sandboxes block all outgoing traffic by default. We open one path, for this sandbox only. (This assumes the runner’s default policy is deny-all; on a balanced or open default, set the default to deny-all first.).

According to recent reports, the allow target (localhost:11434) and the address BuaJi dials (host.docker.internal:11434) are two names for the same runner port,  the first from the runner’s point of view, the second from inside the microVM. Kubernetes, your cloud APIs, and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have.

Industry observers note that kubernetes, your cloud APIs and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have.

BuaJi runs as before, just in a latest place with only two variables:.

The review is now just text. BuaJi cannot post it, act on it, or change what happens to it next.

This check would have caught the fake report in seconds. It runs on the runner, so BuaJi cannot skip it.

It looks up every CVE ID in the NVD database and fails the job if any of them do not exist:.

According to recent reports, because the job is allow_failure: true, GitLab marks it “passed with warnings.” The pipeline keeps moving, but nobody mistakes the report for a trusted one. This degrades the signal, it does not block the human. The warning is a nudge, not a guardrail ~ a tired on-call engineer can still scroll past it..

It won’t catch every made-up detail, like a fake Kubernetes resource name. But it catches the one that holds most fake reports together.

Finally, review the policy log and remove the sandbox:.

Recent findings suggest that the log shows every host BuaJi tried to reach. On a deny-all runner, a healthy run shows only the model on port 11434. Anything else is a signal worth looking at.

Removing the sandbox means every pipeline starts clean.

Put together, the buaji job in .gitlab-ci.yml looks like this:.

The runner needs a GPU and KVM, which usually means self-hosted. GIT_DEPTH: "2" gives buaji.py the two commits it compares. The cleanup sits in after_script, so it runs even when the job fails.

Before, the read-only rule lived in the script. Now it lives in the environment: a read-only checkout, one network path, no credentials, and only checked text coming out.

What hasn’t changed is the human reading the output. The sandbox stops BuaJi from running its scripts. Only the CVE check and a careful reader stop someone else from running them.

Treat an agent’s security finding as a hypothesis, not a conclusion. A report from an AI reviewer is a claim with good formatting. When a human reviewer flags a security issue, there is an implied step where they checked their reasoning. With an agent, that step has not happened, so you have to do it yourself.

Verify every CVE number before acting on it. This is the cheapest check in the whole process and it catches the single most convincing part of a fabricated report. Automate it, as in Step 7, so it runs on every review without anyone having to remember.

It has been revealed that never run agent-written remediation without reviewing it first. Scripts and commands supplied by an agent are the point where a false finding turns into a real incident. Read them with the same care you would give an unknown script from the internet.

Sources indicate that make read-only a property of the environment, not a habit. A restriction you enforce by hand in a pipeline config is always one rushed change away from disappearing. Mount the code read-only, pass in no credentials, and open only the network paths the agent needs, as in Steps 4 to 6.

Clearly label agent review output as agent output. When a bot’s review looks identical to one from a senior engineer, it borrows authority it has not earned. A clear label helps readers apply the right level of skepticism.

Recent findings suggest that keep an eye on your signal-to-noise ratio. The curl story is the warning here. A review channel that fills up with noise eventually stops being read, and a review channel nobody reads is worse than having none, because people still assume it is protecting them.

Sources indicate that the engineer who built BuaJi was right that the read-only rule protected him, and it genuinely did. BuaJi could not touch the cluster, could not revoke anyone’s access, and could not run a single line of the code it had so carefully written. What the rule could not do was stop BuaJi from asking somebody else to run it.

Every other story in this series has been about an agent reaching too far. This one never reached at all. It stayed inside its boundary, did exactly what it was permitted to do, and still produced a document that would have caused a real outage if the person reading it had been a little more tired, or a little less familiar with their own cluster.

As we give agents more responsibility in our pipelines, containing what they can do is only half the job. A sandbox handles that half. The other half is deciding how much we trust what they tell us, and that part is still up to us.

Ajeet Singh Raina, Developer Advocate at Docker, writes and speaks on containers, Docker Compose & AI, helping devs build confidently.

Docker’s WeAreDevelopers keynote demonstrates how Sandboxes, Kits, and Cloud Sandboxes give AI agents strong isolation and reproducible authority.

Profiling in PyTorch (Part 3): Attention is all you profile

📅 10 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is the third post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:.
  • The series "Profiling in PyTorch" is meant to make you comfortable reading profiler traces and tables.
  • In Part 2 we wrapped that addition and multiplication into a torch linear layer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the third post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:.

The series "Profiling in PyTorch" is meant to make you comfortable reading profiler traces and tables. In Part 1 we profiled basic math operations like addition and multiplication. We saw how the profiler table uncovers hotspots, and how the profiler trace shows the order in which an algorithm runs over time.

In Part 2 we wrapped that addition and multiplication into a torch linear layer. We then stacked several linear layers on top of each other (a multilayer perceptron) and profiled that. Along the way we also profiled fused and hand-tuned kernels.

From the perspective of the Transformer architecture, the next logical step for us to profile is yet another fundamental algorithm, attention. While being infamous for its quadratic-time complexity, many clever tricks exist to mitigate that matter and make it fast. Our goal here is not to cover every trick in detail. Instead, we want to see how each one looks different under the profiler.

In a recent development, the scripts for this blog post live here: 04_a_naive_attention.py, 04_b_inplace_ops_attention.py, 04_c_sdpa_attention.py, and 04_d_kernels_attention.py. Like before, it helps to open them in a separate tab and walk through the code as you read. We use an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU to run the scripts. It is really easy to set up a GPU on the Hugging Face infrastructure and experiment with the scripts using Dev Mode with Spaces. One could also run the scripts with the Hugging Face Jobs pipeline.

Industry observers note that attention works with Queries (q), Keys (k), and Values (v). The interaction between them can be written as a short sequence of steps:.

Recent findings suggest that so attention is really a collection of primitive operations. Some of them we already know (the matmuls), and the rest are easy to spot. Let's write a naive attention module in PyTorch and profile it.

Before opening the trace, let's do our usual exercise and guess what we should see. Tracing the forward of this module, we expect:.

Figure 1 indicates the CPU lane of the profile (the GPU lane is folded so it does not overwhelm us). Inside attn_fwd (our annotated forward call) we can see exactly the operations we guessed. The matmul is an old friend by now, and the latest operations are easy to spot:.

Now let's unfold the GPU lane and see which kernels were actually released.

Figure 2 demonstrates the GPU lane next to the CPU lane. Let's zoom into a single attn_fwd block on the GPU lane to look at the kernels one by one.

Figure 3 lets us read off the individual kernels for one profiler step:.

Five of these are expected. The memory copy is the odd one out, so where does this come from? The clue is that PyTorch has in-place operations. When you operate on a tensor the ordinary (out-of-place) way, PyTorch often makes a copy, applies the requested operation to it, and returns the copy. Following the sequence of operations, the culprit here is our masked_fill.

What if we replaced this with an in-place operation?

All we change is masked_fill to masked_fill_ (note the trailing underscore, PyTorch's convention for in-place operations), and we run the same script.

Let's look at the trace and see if something changed.

The in-place version (Figure 5) wraps far fewer CPU ops inside the masking step than the out-of-place version (Figure 4). This is an encouraging signal. Let's unfold the GPU lane to confirm what happened there.

On the GPU lane the Memcpy kernel is gone for good (Figures 6 and 7). With a one line change we shaved a whole kernel off each forward pass. This may not look like much on its own, but remember this is a single attention operation. In the context of a transformer based large model (LLMs, Diffusion models, etc.), it repeats once per layer, and there are many layers, so the saving adds up quickly (and if it earns you a raise, sharing at least 10% with us feels only fair).

Out-of-place is PyTorch's default for a reason. To compute gradients, autograd has to remember the tensor values it saw on the forward pass, because many backward formulas reuse them. An in-place operation overwrites those values in memory, so the backward pass would read the wrong numbers. Due to the fact that we run forward under torch.no_grad, in-place is safe for us, with no backward pass and nothing to corrupt. It is also noteworthy that in-place operations do not only save time (like we see in our case) but also memory (due to no extra copy) which is great for large tensors like logits!

We just built attention from primitives, and even shaved off a Memcpy. The good news is that the PyTorch team has done all of this for us, and packaged the whole pipeline into a single function:.

This one line replaces our hand written module, and is_causal=True even saves us from building the mask by hand. It is worth pausing to appreciate how much this one call hides. And it hides more than just code lines. Scaled Dot Product Attention (SDPA) does not have a single implementation. Under the hood it dispatches to one of the several backends and picks the fastest one that supports our inputs (dtype, head dimension, mask, hardware, etc.).

The official SDPA tutorial walks us through this selection, and the backends themselves are listed in the torch.nn.attention.SDPBackend enum:.

Normally SDPA chooses for us, but we can pin a specific backend with the torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel context manager. This is what we do in our scripts. This lets us profile each backend on its own and read how differently they show up in the trace. Let's go one at a time.

Sources indicate that before we open anything, let's guess. We have replaced hand written attention (matmul, mul, mask, softmax, matmul) with a single one liner, so we should expect the trace to get simpler and faster. Fewer kernels, less CPU dispatch, maybe even a fused kernel. Let's check the profiler table first.

This is our first surprise, the one liner is 3.7x slower.

Opening the trace (Figure 9) indicates why the alarm bells ring, the math backend launches 20 GPU kernels per forward instead of the 5 released with our naive attention implementation (Figure 8). This is the opposite of what we guessed. Let's figure out why this happens.

Recent findings suggest that in Part 2 we learned to read a kernel name like a fingerprint. Let's use that habit here:.

The A100s we used to capture these traces ship with Tensor Cores, specialised hardware for accelerated matmuls that is known to be far faster than the ordinary CUDA cores. To see why that matters here, it helps to know what lives inside a GPU. A Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) is the compute unit of a GPU, and each SM has two kinds of arithmetic units, the CUDA cores and the Tensor Cores. CUDA cores are general purpose and process a handful of elements at a time, while Tensor Cores multiply and accumulate a whole small matrix tile in a single instruction. So the question is simple, "Is each backend actually using the fast path?".

The kernel names answer it. The s16816 in the naive kernel (Figure 10) is the signature of a bfloat16 Tensor Core matmul (the 16x8x16 Tensor Core instruction), so the naive version is on the fast path. sgemm (Figure 11) is the classic single precision (FP32) matmul that runs on the ordinary CUDA cores. In other words, the math backend never touches the Tensor Cores at all: to trade speed for numerical accuracy it upcasts tensors to FP32 (doubling the data moved, even when the inputs are in bf16) and falls back to the slower CUDA cores.

In the naive version we built the causal mask once and reused it. Here we passed is_causal=True and the math backend materialized one for us, on every single call. You can watch it happen on the CPU lane:.

Here is what we see in Figure 12.

Sources indicate that on the GPU this shows up as a triu_tril_kernel, several where kernels, and an add_. The convenience flag that let us stop thinking about the mask did not remove the work, it just moved it one layer down, where the mask is rebuilt from scratch every forward.

Our hand written version called plain aten::softmax. The math backend calls aten::_safe_softmax, and the difference is again visible as extra kernels (Figure 13):.

Sources indicate that A row that is fully masked (every entry -inf) would make an ordinary softmax compute exp(-inf)/sum(exp(-inf)) = 0/0 = NaN. _safe_softmax guards against exactly that. Our naive kernel never bothered, and would have quietly produced NaNs in that corner case.

Industry observers note that put together, the math backend is the reference implementation. It is a straightforward, dtype-safe, NaN-safe decomposition of attention into primitive ATen ops. It is essentially the naive attention we wrote by hand, but more careful. That carefulness is exactly what makes it extremely slow.

Industry observers note that its job is not to be fast, but to always work. This makes it the perfect baseline. Every backend we profile next (flash, efficient, cudnn) is trying to collapse the 20 GPU kernels into essentially one fused kernel that stays in bf16 and never materializes the intermediate matrices at all.

Where the math backend launched 20 kernels across one profiler step, the efficient backend debuts only one fmha_cutlassF_bf16_aligned_64x64_rf_sm80 (as seen in Figure 14).

Let's decode the name of the kernel:.

It has been revealed that this is the memory efficient attention kernel that grew out of Meta's xformers library and was upstreamed into PyTorch. When people say "the xformers backend," this fmha_cutlassF kernel is what they mean.

The void pytorch_flash kernel (Figure 15) is FlashAttention-2 (Tri Dao's implementation), vendored into PyTorch.

Before we read the trace any further, it is worth answering the question you should be asking by now: why is there a whole backend named "flash", and why does it matter so much?

Industry observers note that let's go back to the math backend for a moment. Its real problem was not the count of 20 kernels, it was what those kernels handed to each other.

Step 1 builds the full score matrix attn = q . k.T, which is [seq, seq] per head. For a sequence length of 4096 that is 4096 x 4096 ≈ 16 million numbers for a single head. That matrix is written out to the HBM (the GPU's main memory), if there is even enough space to do so. Then, it is read back to be scaled, written again for the mask, read again for the softmax, and so on. Attention's cost is dominated by this back and forth traffic to HBM, not by the matmuls themselves.

According to recent reports, flashAttention attacks exactly this. Instead of computing the whole s matrix and only then reducing it, it walks over k and v in tiles, keeps a running softmax as it goes (the "online softmax" trick), and accumulates the output one tile at a time. The full [seq, seq] score matrix is never written to HBM, it only ever lives on-chip. This is the single idea that lets the entire attention pipeline collapse into one fused kernel that stays in bf16 on the Tensor cores.

Here is where flash surprises people who read profiler footprints. It is the fastest backend, yet the profiler reports it with very low occupancy (shown in Figure 16). To see why that is fine, we need three quick definitions.

Sources indicate that A GPU kernel is essentially a series of instructions executed by many small execution units. These individual execution units (threads) take care of loading variables, adding them together, storing them back, etc. For each kernel, we launch many, many threads, and to keep track of them, we group them by blocks.

Blocks are scheduled onto Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), the main compute units of a GPU. A block lives entirely on one SM, and an SM can host multiple blocks at once if it has enough resources. Those resources include registers, shared memory, maximum resident threads, and maximum resident warps. So when we say a kernel has low occupancy, we mean each SM has fewer resident warps than it could theoretically support.

Sources indicate that if you want to know more about threads, blocks, grids, etc. here is a great resource.

If you click the flash kernel in the trace, its footprint tells the story (Figure 17).

Recent findings suggest that flash uses a lot of per-thread registers and a large amount of shared memory per block. For example, if a block has 128 threads and each thread uses 255 registers, that block needs 128 × 255 = 32,640 registers. On an Ampere SM with 65,536 registers, only two such blocks fit at once. Each 128-thread block has 128 / 32 = 4 warps, so two blocks give only 8 resident warps. Against a maximum of 64 resident warps, that is roughly 13% occupancy. Flash has low occupancy not because it is poorly optimized, but because each block is deliberately very "heavy" in on-chip resource usage.

And that is the whole point. High occupancy helps hide latency by keeping many warps ready to run, but it does not make the work itself efficient. Flash spends those registers and that shared memory on purpose, to keep attention tiles on-chip, reuse data aggressively, and avoid ever materializing the full attention matrix in global memory.

By now the pattern is familiar. Like flash and efficient, cuDNN gives us one fused, flash-style kernel per forward (Figure 18). So the natural question is: if flash already fuses attention, why does PyTorch ship yet another flash backend? The answer is who writes the kernel and how it is built, and that difference is what makes the trace look different.

In a recent development, flash and efficient are fixed, pre-compiled kernels vendored into PyTorch. You get the same binary every time. cuDNN is NVIDIA's own deep learning library, and its attention kernel is generated and tuned for the specific problem at hand. It is closer in spirit to torch.compile's codegen than to a fixed cuBLAS binary. You can read that straight off the (very long) kernel name:.

That one fact, generated per problem, explains everything else that looks unusual in the trace.

In a recent development, no transposes: The CPU lane goes from _cudnn_attention_forward straight to a couple of aten::empty allocations and then the kernel, with zero aten::transpose (Figures 19, 20 and 21). Flash and efficient each insert four (metadata) transposes to reshape the tensors while cuDNN consumes the native [B, H, S, D] layout directly because its generator emits a kernel for that layout.

In a recent development, it rolls out through cuLaunchKernelEx, not cudaLaunchKernel: Every other kernel in this whole series went through the runtime API cudaLaunchKernel. cuDNN uses the driver-level extended launch, which carries launch attributes (Figure 22).

The profiler reports 0% achieved occupancy: Do not take that at face value, it is a measurement gap, not a stalled GPU. CUPTI (the profiling backend) cannot attribute occupancy to a driver-API (cuLaunchKernelEx) launch the way it does for cudaLaunchKernel, so the field reads 0. The footprint fills in the truth (Figure 23): 240 registers × 256 threads = 61,440 registers per block against the SM's 65,536, so only one block fits per SM (8 warps ≈ 12.5%), right in line with flash.

The "no transposes" story tempts us to expect cuDNN to be the leanest backend on the CPU. It is the opposite.

Even with zero transpose ops, cuDNN spends about 214 µs per forward on the CPU, more than flash (138) or efficient (117). Almost all of it sits in aten::scaled_dot_product_attention self time (26% of the whole run) and _cudnn_attention_forward. That is cuDNN's runtime engine selecting and preparing the proposal (the "knob" search) on every call.

Sources indicate that fewer visible ATen ops did not mean less CPU work, it moved the work into the library, where the profiler can only show it as one fat, opaque bar. When a trace suddenly gets cleaner, the work has not always disappeared, sometimes it has just moved somewhere the profiler cannot break down.

Recent findings suggest that on the GPU, cuDNN (186.3 µs) lands between efficient and flash. On this very flash-friendly shape, hand-written FlashAttention-2 edges it out. cuDNN often wins on other shapes (larger head dimensions, different sequence lengths) precisely because its generator retunes per problem, but that retuning is also what you just paid for on the CPU.

Before we wrap up, here is a single table to review every attention variant we profiled and the one lesson each trace taught us.

If you take away only one thing from the whole series, let it be the habit we repeated before every single trace which is to guess first, then look.

State out loud what you expect the trace to contain, open it, and treat any mismatch as the most interesting thing on the screen. Every real insight in these three posts, the hidden Memcpy, the addmm epilogue, the 20 kernel math backend, flash's "wrong-looking" occupancy, cuDNN's fat CPU bar, came from a guess that did not match the trace.

Industry observers note that profiling is not a separate, intimidating skill reserved for GPU experts. It is just the discipline of looking closely and asking "wait, why is that happening?" until the answer clicks. You now have the vocabulary and the reflexes to do that on your own models. Open a trace, form a guess, and go find the mismatch.

Thanks for reading the Profiling in PyTorch series. Now go profile something. 🤗.

Thanks to Noe Flandre for their reviews on the early draft of the post!

In a recent development, the blog post was polished using an LLM. This in no way means that we have let an agent run in the background and let it generate the blog. Some of us in the team are non-english speakers and think LLMs (which are mostly trained in the English Language) can rectify silly grammar mistakes or rephrase sentences that sound less intimidating and cleaner. Hope this helps with the idea of "why should I read, if this was LLM generated". 🤗.

Thanks for the series, really delightful!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Giving an agent a sandbox also means deciding which files it will work on.
  • Sources indicate that you might want to watch the diff in your local editor and make changes alongside the agent, or give it room to manage several tasks while you review the results.
  • Industry observers note that sharing a checkout puts the agent in the working tree you already use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Giving an agent a sandbox also means deciding which files it will work on. You can share a checkout from your host, give it a separate working directory for a task, or keep the repository entirely inside the sandbox. Each arrangement changes how you, the human, participate in the work.

Sources indicate that you might want to watch the diff in your local editor and make changes alongside the agent, or give it room to manage several tasks while you review the results. sbx supports both. The way you organize the checkout can change as you ask the agent to take on more of the work.

Industry observers note that sharing a checkout puts the agent in the working tree you already use. Run sbx run from your project directory, and it mounts that directory at the same absolute path inside the sandbox:.

Open a file in your local editor while the agent works on it, and you’ll see changes as they happen. Git works from either side, so you choose whether you want to let the agent make commits or you do it yourself. Development servers on your host can pick up the edits through hot reload, using the runtime and dependencies installed on your host.

It has been revealed that this fits close collaboration on one task. The coordination cost comes from sharing that working tree: switching branches changes the files the agent sees, and your edits become part of its ongoing work. If you want to switch to something unrelated while the agent continues, you’ll need another checkout.

NOTE: Dependencies written into the shared checkout are shared too. Packages with native binaries, such as esbuild, may work in the Linux sandbox and fail on a macOS or Windows host. Reinstalling on the host can reverse the problem. Keep separate dependency installations, or run the app consistently in one environment.

According to recent reports, git worktrees give each task a directory and branch. You can mount each worktree in its own sandbox, while your original checkout remains available for other work. The agent’s edits appear in the worktree. You can inspect either with your local editor and development tools. Each task also gets its own running environment, with tools to prepare and a sandbox and worktree to clean up afterward.

Sources indicate that there is a Git limitation with mounting only a linked worktree. Its .git file points to metadata outside the mount, which the agent can’t reach. It can edit files, but checking status, branching, and committing have to happen on the host. The future of software development still needs you to run git status.

It has been revealed that sbx supports a clone mode that gives the agent a separate checkout with Git available inside the sandbox. You keep your local project, but sbx mounts the host source as read-only and creates an independent clone for the agent. Its branch changes and dependency installations stay in its checkout.

Bringing the result back becomes a handoff. While the sandbox is running, you can fetch committed branches through the Git remote sbx adds on your host. Or the agent can push to the repository’s remote and you can retrieve the branch through your usual Git workflow. Your local editor and development server see the changes after you bring them into your checkout.

A mountless sandbox has no host workspace directory attached. Clone the repository inside it, and the sandbox holds the checkout and its development environment. Your host copy of the project shares no connection with the sandbox checkout.

This workflow resembles working on a remote development machine. Agents connect to the project environment, and you can open a shell with sbx exec or connect an editor to the sandbox over SSH. Changes and dependency installations stay separate from your host. To bring work back, you push a branch to the Git remote.

It has been revealed that one sandbox per project can be a useful mental model here. The project and its tools persist across agent sessions and sandbox restarts. An agent can create worktrees per feature it’s working on, push branches, and create pull requests for review. Starting another task doesn’t require you to prepare another host worktree and sandbox, and the agent has Git access in each working directory. Clone mode supports this internal-worktree approach too.

It has been revealed that those tasks share tools and services, so running servers or changing the environment still needs coordination. Separate sandboxes are useful when tasks need independent environments as well as separate files. Branches alone don’t isolate simultaneous edits in one working directory.

In a recent development, that independence adds some distance when you want to try the result. Your usual local editor isn’t looking at these files, and a development server running inside the sandbox needs a published port to reach it from your browser.

For a web app preview, ask the agent:.

Start the development server on port 8080, bound to 0.0.0.0.

Then publish the port from another terminal on the host:.

Open http://localhost:8080 in your browser. It’s possible to work interactively this way, but there’s more ceremony than opening a project already on your filesystem.

An environment file can make setup repeatable, selecting tools and cloning the repository at creation with something like the community github-clone kit. Recreating the sandbox then gives you a fresh environment. Push or copy out work you want to retain first: removing a sandbox deletes files held only there.

According to recent reports, an API change might need a corresponding frontend change, or another repository might provide useful reference material. You can mount several directories into one sandbox, with read-only access for reference repositories. Local editing and previews remain available, but each writable checkout needs branch and change coordination. Task-specific checkouts also leave directories to clean up afterward.

A workspace manager such as jganoff/wsp can assemble selected repositories for a task. Mounting that workspace gives the agent the projects it needs together. These are standard clones with their own Git metadata, so the agent retains Git access, unlike a mounted linked worktree.

The same scope fits inside a mountless sandbox: clone the repositories needed there and keep the whole workspace in the sandbox. The number of repositories and where their files live are separate choices.

The checkout’s location, the sandbox’s lifetime, and the repositories it contains are choices you can combine. You can keep a project sandbox around for many tasks, or mount a workspace assembled for one job. What suits you may change when you want to work more closely with the agent, or give it more room to manage the work itself.

The Git workflows documentation covers the mechanics of direct mounts, clone mode, and host worktrees.

It has been revealed that give AI coding agents live web access with the Firecrawl kit for Docker Sandboxes. Learn to search, scrape, and crawl websites with network controls.

A container shares the host kernel. Docker Sandboxes are microVMs with their own kernel and private Docker Engine. See how they differ and when to use each.
